rows.source: HSE control of lead at work
rows.verified: Employers must prevent employee exposure to lead or, where that is not reasonably practicable, control it.

rows.source: HSE control of lead at work
rows.verified: The occupational exposure limit for lead in air stated by HSE is 0.15 milligrams per cubic metre.

rows.source: HSE control of lead at work
rows.verified: HSE lists blood-lead suspension levels of 60 micrograms per decilitre for males and 30 for females.

rows.source: HSE control of lead at work
rows.verified: The blood-lead suspension level for workers under 18 is listed as 50 micrograms per decilitre.

rows.source: HSE control of lead at work
rows.verified: Health effects observed at elevated blood-lead levels include changes in blood, nervous-system effects and kidney effects.

rows.source: HSE control of lead at work
rows.verified: Lead exposure can also affect male reproductive function and has been associated with elevated blood pressure.

rows.source: HSE control of lead at work
rows.verified: Lead may present an inhalation, ingestion or skin-absorption hazard depending on its form.

rows.source: HSE control of lead at work
rows.verified: Construction risk assessment should identify tasks that use lead or create lead dust or fume, including work on older leaded paint.

rows.source: HSE control of lead at work
rows.verified: Lead risk depends on chemical form, airborne level, ingestion route, task, hygiene, controls, worker factors and exposure duration.

rows.source: HSE control of lead at work
rows.verified: HSE lead evidence is substance-, worker-, task-, exposure-, monitoring-, control- and time-specific and is not a parcel-level toxicity probability.
HSE compressed-air guidance addresses designers, manufacturers, installers and users of compressor systems.
Headline hazards include bodily entry of compressed air, skin penetration, explosions and eye damage from particles.
Overpressurisation is identified as a major compressed-air hazard.
Blockages and failures of automatic controls can contribute to overpressurisation.
Overspeeding and nearby external fires are listed among associated hazards.
Overheating and deposit accumulation can increase risk in compressed-air systems.
The guidance covers compressor plant, air receivers, dryers, coolers, main lines, actuators and portable pneumatic tools.
Inspection, maintenance and training are identified as general safety needs.
Compressed-air risk depends on pressure, equipment design, guarding, hose condition, blockage, maintenance, operator behaviour and environment.
HSE compressed-air evidence is system-, equipment-, operator-, maintenance-, control- and time-specific and is not a parcel-level injury probability.
UKHSA contact-tracing guidance supports risk assessment and categorisation of contacts of confirmed mpox cases.
Contact categories are used to determine appropriate follow-up, public-health and isolation advice.
Home-isolation guidance includes measures to reduce transmission within a household.
Separate cleaning guidance is provided for the isolation period and for the end of isolation.
UKHSA guidance distinguishes the two main mpox clades, clade I and clade II.
Healthcare providers should conduct local risk assessments where suspected or confirmed mpox cases may be encountered.
Risk assessments should be completed by a competent person and communicated to relevant workers.
UK public-health guidance includes case management, contact management, PPE, cleaning, vaccination and surveillance resources.
Mpox risk depends on clade, symptoms, contact type, exposure intensity, setting, host vulnerability, controls and timing.
UKHSA mpox evidence is case-, contact-, setting-, clade-, intervention- and time-specific and is not a parcel-level infection probability.
